title: When costs outrun wages, work shifts from mobility strategy to survival strategy
source_unit: Federal Reserve Worker Perspectives Project, When Every Dollar Counts: Inside the Economic Struggles of Workers Who Earn Low to Moderate Incomes, 2026; 11 focus groups conducted with Ipsos in late 2025
geography: United States; low- to moderate-income households with annual household income of $85,000 or less

denominator.unit: participants in 11 U.S. focus groups, including Spanish-language sessions

income_threshold.unit: annual household income threshold for inclusion, approximately half of U.S. households

survival_vs_success.value: participants described a stronger focus on survival, cost pressure, and financial stress in 2025 than in the 2022 research

four_report_themes.value: survival mode; constrained upward mobility; job search and job-quality tradeoffs; perseverance amid low macro confidence

observations.method: Qualitative focus-group research recruited across the United States; the report is designed to explain the why, what, and how behind aggregate labor-market and household trends.
observations.uncertainty: The 63 participants are not a probability sample and their comments cannot estimate national prevalence, average income effects, or causal labor-market outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Workers and job seekers in low- to moderate-income households; household sizes and employment situations vary.
observations.counterinterpretation: Focus-group language may emphasize hardship, and changes from 2022 may reflect different participants, economic context, question framing, or recall rather than a population-wide shift.

observations.period: 2025 compared with 2022; economic mobility and employment risk

denominator.unit: author-reported qualitative comparison across Worker Perspectives focus-group rounds

mobility_strategy_shift.value: in 2022 many participants were more willing to leave jobs, pursue credentials, or consider self-employment; in 2025 many were less willing to risk a change and focused on maintaining income

education_and_skill_barrier.value: few participants pursued education; cost, childcare, work-school balance, and uncertainty about returns were recurring barriers

job_hugging.value: employed participants often stayed in imperfect jobs because equivalent or better opportunities felt difficult to find

observations.method: Comparative qualitative synthesis of Worker Perspectives focus groups conducted in 2022 and 2025.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is not a longitudinal panel of the same participants and cannot quantify the share of workers changing behavior or identify a single cause.
observations.subgroup: LMI workers and job seekers represented in the two focus-group rounds.
observations.counterinterpretation: Staying in a job can reflect satisfaction, caregiving, geographic limits, benefits, or risk preferences as well as weakened mobility; pursuing education may be delayed rather than abandoned.

side_hustle_function.value: formal gig work and informal side work were described primarily as ways to cover costs or bridge unemployment, not as durable self-employment pathways

survival_coping.value: participants described changing consumption, extending credit, and relying on formal or informal safety nets to make ends meet

long_term_tradeoff.value: month-to-month necessities crowded out savings, education, skill-building, and longer-arc career investment

observations.method: Qualitative coding and synthesis of participant accounts of household budgets, employment changes, side work, credit, and support networks.
observations.uncertainty: The report captures perceived strategies and experiences, not verified income, spending, debt, hours, or later household outcomes.
observations.subgroup: LMI participants experiencing employment or cost pressure; coping routes differ by household and work situation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Side work can provide agency, networking, or future business opportunities for some participants; informal support can be protective rather than evidence of failure.

compensation_priority.value: adequate compensation was foundational because participants needed income to meet household necessities

flexibility_and_care.value: flexibility, work-life balance, and time for caregiving, family, and self-care remained important

quality_as_aspiration.value: in 2025 job-quality features were more often described as aspirational or nice to have than as conditions that would determine whether participants accepted or left a job

observations.method: Qualitative comparison of how participants described compensation, benefits, flexibility, advancement, culture, meaning, and work-life balance in job decisions.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not rank job-quality attributes with a representative choice experiment or observe actual offers, schedules, wages, or turnover.
observations.subgroup: LMI workers and job seekers, including caregivers and people in unstable employment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some workers may reject jobs for nonfinancial reasons or value flexibility over pay; the reported shift may reflect labor-market scarcity rather than a permanent change in preferences.

ai_screening_barrier.value: many active job seekers perceived AI screening and automated interviews as making it harder to reach human consideration

job_scam_exposure.value: some participants described suspected or experienced job scams that sought information or money

confidence_effect.value: technology-mediated screening and nonresponse compounded uncertainty and reduced confidence in navigating the labor market

observations.method: Qualitative accounts of applications, employer response, AI interaction, automated screening, and suspected job scams.
observations.uncertainty: Participants’ perceptions do not establish how often AI actually screened them out, whether screening was accurate, or the prevalence of job scams nationally.
observations.subgroup: Participants actively or passively searching for jobs in LMI households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Automated tools can improve matching, reduce employer burden, or detect fraud; lack of response can also reflect labor-market volume or employer practices unrelated to AI.

related_sources.claim: DOI and citation record for the Federal Reserve Worker Perspectives report.
Federal Reserve SHED employment and job-quality statistics provide quantitative context but are not pooled with this qualitative study.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. lived-experience mechanism behind labor-market and household-security trends: cost pressure can shift workers from mobility and long-term investment toward survival, job retention, side work, and defensive search behavior. It is a qualitative focus-group study, not a nationally representative prevalence estimate, longitudinal panel, or causal evaluation of AI, wages, or employment policy.
